history.alt_text: An unbranded developer workstation chassis with a plugin cartridge half-inserted into an agent bay on a concrete floor.
history.caption: A plugin cartridge slides into an unlisted agent slot on a developer workstation, silently expanding the cost beyond the purchased seat count.
history.title: Silent agent hook in developer workstation

style_when: the news is structural and abstract — a stack reordered, a layer added, a flow rerouted — and there is no literal object that carries it, so the idea is stated as a small physical assembly of recognisable parts rather than as bare shapes
prompt: Matte clay model of an unbranded developer workstation chassis on a weathered concrete floor in a dark server room. The chassis is an open clamshell with a slotted modular agent bay; a bone white plugin cartridge with two copper contact pins is half-inserted into the left slot; a second empty steel slot sits to its right, and a latched graphite cover hangs ajar. Low raking light from the left casts long contact shadows, extreme asymmetry with the assembly off-centre left and generous empty right margin, matte graphite, bone white, and copper palette, no text, no labels, no screen characters.
negative_prompt: garbled text, random lettering, watermarks, UI, labels, screen characters, numbers
rationale: The story is structural and abstract: a desktop app modifies agent settings, creating a gap between seats and agents. A matte clay 3D render lets us state that mechanism as a small mechanical assembly — a plugin entering a workstation bay — without falling into generic screenshots or datacenter clichés.
cue: the app quietly changed two coding agents
subject: an unbranded developer workstation chassis with a plugin cartridge entering a modular agent bay
core_thesis: A desktop developer tool now installs itself into the coding agents on a workstation, so the real cost of buying it is counted in agent settings your inventory does not list and priced in agents your seat count does not cover.
core_conflict: The published per-user seat license collides with the actual agent count silently added to each developer's workstation, so purchasing and inventory no longer describe the same fleet.
composition: extreme asymmetry, hero assembly off-centre left, empty right side for editorial negative space
alt_text: A grey clay-rendered server chassis with an open side panel and a plugin cartridge half-inserted, on a concrete floor before a rack row.
caption: An unbranded chassis with a plugin cartridge half-inserted: the client plants its plugin where the agent reads its instructions.
title: Postman Hooks Your Coding Agents

review.depicts: A matte-rendered, doorless grey box-chassis sits slightly left of centre on a cracked concrete floor, with a pale plug-like cartridge carrying two copper pins slid into a slot on its open left side, a hinged lid leaning against its right flank, and dark server racks standing in the dim background.
review.reason: The cartridge entering a modular bay is the article's own mechanism — a plugin being installed into an agent slot on a workstation — so the metaphor lands, though the unbranded clay-like chassis reads somewhat generically as hardware rather than specifically as coding agents.
